analysis.one_liner: Extends minimum wage, overtime, and safety rules to traveling door-to-door sales crews and bans minors from the work.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted traveling sales crews — groups of salespeople, often young and far from home, who travel together to sell door to door. It would have removed their exemption from federal minimum wage and overtime rules, barred anyone under 18 from door-to-door work requiring overnight travel, and required crew employers and supervisors to register with the Labor Department, carry vehicle insurance, meet housing and transport safety standards, and disclose pay and work terms to recruits. Employers who violated the rules would face fines, criminal penalties, and private lawsuits. The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Traveling sales crew workers — disproportionately teenagers and young adults, many recruited from far away — would gain guaranteed minimum wage and overtime, written disclosure of pay and deductions, a ban on charging them business expenses like van upkeep, insured and safety-inspected vehicles, health-certified housing, and the right to sue abusive employers with attorney's fees covered.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 'outside salesman' exemption for crew members who travel and do not return home nightly, so federal minimum wage and overtime rules would apply to them
Bars anyone under 18 from door-to-door sales or related support work that keeps them away from home more than 24 hours

Requires crew employers and supervisors to obtain annual Labor Department registration certificates, including fingerprints and disclosure of every vehicle and housing facility used, with refusal or revocation for serious criminal history or past violations
Obliges employers to give written disclosures of wages, costs charged to workers, and workers' compensation coverage, keep three years of payroll records, and pay wages in cash or by check when due

Bans employers from making workers buy goods solely from the employer or charging them business expenses like vehicle costs, and requires vehicle insurance and Secretary-prescribed vehicle safety standards

Creates criminal penalties up to one year in prison for a first willful violation and three years for repeat violations, civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation, and a private right of action with attorney's fees for aggrieved workers
Prohibits employers from intimidating, blacklisting, or firing workers who file complaints or testify, with reinstatement and back pay available

analysis.who_pays: Traveling sales crew operators and the companies whose products they sell. They would bear a $500 annual employer registration fee (plus $50 per supervisor), vehicle insurance and safety-standard costs, health-certified housing, and higher payroll costs from minimum wage and overtime coverage. Some marginal operators might exit the business or pass costs along.

drawbacks.text: The registration scheme imposes real compliance costs — a $500 annual employer fee, $50 per supervisor, fingerprints, vehicle and housing documentation, and annual renewals — which small legitimate operators would pay alongside large ones

Applying minimum wage and overtime to traveling crews raises payroll costs for a business model that has often relied on commission-only pay, which could reduce the number of crew jobs, including for the young workers the bill aims to protect

The bill leaves many standards to Labor Department rulemaking — vehicle safety levels, insurance amounts, bonding, and 'any other requirement' the Secretary may establish — giving one agency wide discretion over the industry's operating terms

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address serious documented harms to a vulnerable, often underage workforce — unpaid wages, crews stranded without pay or transport, and van crashes. The compliance costs fall on a small, specific industry rather than the general public, though the registration burden is heavy enough that marginal operators could fold, and there is a real tension between protecting workers and eliminating the low-wage jobs some of them currently hold.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Herb Kohl introduced the Traveling Sales Crew Protection Act on January 22, 2001
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
Three Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill
The bill's entire recorded action history is introduction, remarks, and referral; it never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the 107th Congress ended

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traveling sales crew operators are better off: they avoided registration fees, insurance mandates, wage and record-keeping rules, and lawsuit exposure. Young crew workers, the intended beneficiaries, gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Herb Kohl
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or reported it, letting it die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democratic initiative — the sponsor and all three cosponsors were Senate Democrats — but no one opposed it on the record, because the committee simply never acted on it.

industries.industry: Traveling sales crew operators and the door-to-door sales industry
industries.note: The bill would have imposed registration, fees, insurance, wage, and record-keeping requirements on a business model that has often run on commission-only pay and young transient labor. Its interest ran against the workers the bill would protect.

industries.industry: Product companies that sell through traveling crews (e.g., magazines, household goods)
industries.note: Companies relying on traveling crews as a sales channel would face higher, more regulated distribution costs, potentially tightening the supply of crew selling. Consumers buying door-to-door would face few direct changes.
